 Adapting to floods through local innovation in Vietnam
 Published: 11 November 2026 
 Reading Time: 4 mins 
 Back 
 Authors
 Thong Anh Tran 
 The Australian National University 
 Back 
 In Brief
 In Vietnam’s Can Tho City, persistent seasonal flooding is prompting urban communities to experiment with practical ways to mitigate its impacts on their businesses and daily life. These initiatives demonstrate how communities organise self-help, mobilise resources and learn from one another, particularly where government support is limited. Governments should incorporate lessons from these grassroots experiments into flood management and urban planning to better respond to local needs.

 Cities are embracing innovative solutions to deal with the wicked problems presented by coupled climate and development challenges. In Can Tho City, the largest city in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta region, seasonal flooding has prompted locals to experiment with practical methods to manage the disruption to their lives and livelihoods.
 Urban experimentation , defined as a process of trialling, discovering and testing, has become a common practice for communities living in areas exposed to climate change.
 Urban communities in Can Tho City have long experienced the challenges posed by floods, with different localities facing varying levels of inundation. Prolonged exposure to flooding disrupts their livelihoods and worsens health conditions .
 Can Tho City’s flooding stems from a variety of factors . Dykes built to support agricultural development in the upper delta, alongside land subsidence and environmental factors like rainfall and tidal systems, have compounded vulnerabilities and exacerbated flooding on a large scale. Some also point to the risk that infrastructure intended to control f looding in central areas can push floodwater outwards , inundating low-lying and unprotected adjacent areas.
 Community initiatives to adapt to floods combine traditional ecological knowledge that has been accumulated over time with innovative approaches.
 Participatory community engagement through storytelling and photovoice activities highlights how community-led adaptation revolves around experimentation. They show how urban communities develop strategies to respond to floods while sustaining their livelihoods during the flood season. These adaptation narratives also reveal how communities organise self-help and mobilise resources to alleviate flood impacts when government support is limited or absent. It is perceived that local governments do not often pay adequate attention to those engaged in informal employment, such as women small-scale traders and street vendors.
 Urban community groups whose livelihoods are directly exposed to flooding employ a range of experiment-based adaptation strategies.
 Young migrant gig workers, who work for ride-hailing and delivery apps, use Vietnamese social media platform Zalo to disseminate flood risk-informed messages and provide urgent assistance when needed. Women street vendors mitigate flood damage by raising merchandise above flood levels and using accessible materials to prevent floodwater from entering homes. Others use flood gauging apparatuses to monitor or anticipate flood levels so that they can reschedule their sale operations to avoid or mitigate flood impacts.
 These community-led experiments are collectively initiated, implemented and disseminated across flood-prone communities, allowing community members to learn from one another.
 Community-led experimentation can serve as vital ‘soft’ infrastructure that complements state-led engineering for flood management. Through experiment-based adaptation, urban communities also showcase their creativity, perseverance and agency in responding to floods, while also amplifying their voices and aspirations for change.
 These experiments should be formally recognised and integrated into long-term institutional urban planning efforts. Local communities could report flood levels and other urgent flood-related developments to government agencies for further action or to inform municipal flood-risk data and early warning systems.
 City governments also need to provide conducive environments for leveraging community-led experimentation and facilitating knowledge integration for improved flood management. Lessons from community experiments could help inform the integration of blue, green and grey infrastructure systems and hydrological models into urban planning to better accommodate local needs.
 Looking ahead, community-led adaptation endeavours can foster momentum for building innovative urban flood adaptation and resilience strategies in the long term. These approaches are especially pertinent amid the accelerating uncertainties and complexities of floods in both Can Tho City and other climate-afflicted cities in ASEAN countries.
 Thong Anh Tran is Honorary Lecturer at Fenner School of Environment and Society, The Australian National University. 
 This article was based on the author’s field study in the CAPE project ‘Climate Action and Participatory Experiments for Urban Resilience in the Philippines and Vietnam’ funded by the CLARE-ASEAN program. More information can be seen through this documentary video as an output of the project.
